senses.gloss:
Kāśī
(‘that which shines [because of spiritual power]’)
------------------------------------------
A पिल्ग्रिमगे to काशी (also known as वाराणसी or Banaras, in the State of Uttar Pradesh), a ceremonial bath in the river गङ्गा and a visit to the temple of Lord Viśvanātha, has always been a lifetime’s ambition for an average Hindu, right from the ancient times. To him काशी has been synonymous with Hindu religion, culture, learning, arts and crafts; in fact, with every aspect of Hindu civilisation. It is the only city in the whole world that has kept up its halo of holiness for over three thousand (or even more number of) years.
काशी">Viśvanātha Temple at KāśīIt is one of the three most holy cities, the other two being प्रयाग and गया.
The पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस् as also the digests have devoted thousands of verses to expatiate upon the greatness of this holy city.
The antiquity of the city is established by the fact that it has been mentioned in the ब्राह्मणस् and the उपनिषद्स् in several places.
It appears that काशी was a country and its capital, वाराणसी. In course of time, the capital too got the same name. Other names of काशी are: Ānandakānana, Avimukta, Mahāśmaśāna and Śmaśāna.
‘Banaras’ is the anglicised form of वाराणसी.
It got the name वाराणसी since it was situated between two rivers Varaṇā and Asī. This is now the official name of the city.
It was established by दिवोदास, a human इन्चर्नतिओन् of the god धन्वन्तरि.
Kāśī is reputed to have had 1500 temples at one time. Most of the temples are in a dilapidated condition.
The most important temples and holy spots which a modern pilgrim normally visits are the following:
The विश्वनाथ तेम्प्ले; the अन्न-pūrṇā temple; the बिन्दु-माधव temple; the Durgiana temple; the temple of सूर्य (Sun-god) at Lolārka; the Daśāśvamedha-ghāṭ; the Maṇikarṇikā-ghāṭ; the Pañcagaṅgā-ghāṭ.
Lord Viśvanātha is the tutelary deity of काशी and his temple is the centre of attraction. Every Hindu of काशी is expected to bathe in the river गङ्गा and visit the temple of Viśvanātha every day.
The विश्वनाथ तेम्प्ले has had a chequered history over the centuries. According to Hiuen Tsang (7th century A. D.) there was a copper image of Deva महेश्वर, almost 30 metres (100 ft.) in height, at काशी. Between A. D. 1194 and 1585 it was destroyed and rebuilt many times. Due to a saintly ब्राह्मण, नारायण भट्ट, it was rebuilt with the help of राजा Todarmal in A. D. 1585. However it was destroyed by Aurangzeb in A. D. 1669 and a mosque was built on its ruin, which is still to be seen. It was अहल्याबाई होऌकर् who built the present temple during the last quarter of the 18th century. This temple is situated in a lane, next to the river गङ्गा. It has a tower covered with gold-plated copper sheets which was the contribution of Mahārājā Raṇajit Siṅgh (A. D. 1780-1839) and is 4.5 metres (50 ft.) high. Only Hindus without caste-distinctions, are permitted inside. Behind the temple is an ancient well called ‘Jñānavāpī’ (well of knowledge) which was repaired in A. D. 1830.
The विश्वनाथ तेम्प्ले is surrounded by several other temples like those of अन्नपूर्णा, दुर्गा, गणेश, Śanaiścara and others.
The बिन्दु-माधव temple is situated in the Pañcagaṅgā-ghāṭ where five rivers—Kiraṇā, Dhūtapāpā, गङ्गा, यमुना and Sarasvatī—meet and merge. However only the गङ्गा is seen and the other four are supposed to join it from below the earth.
The Daśāśvamedha-ghāṭ has been famous for centuries. ब्रह्मा, the creator, is said to have performed ten अश्वमेध sacrifices here.
The Maṇikarṇikā-ghāṭ is, practically, a च्रेमतिओन् ground. Bodies of the dead are cremated here in the belief that शिव liberates their souls. The pool of water here is very small. Near it is the temple of Tārakeśvara-शिव.
The temple of Lolārka (Sun-god) is situated at the confluence of the river Asī with गङ्गा.
Since ages, the Hindus have believed that death at काशी automatically gives them लिबेरतिओन्. Hence, the number of persons, especially the old ones, living here, awaiting death, is quite large.
Those who take a vow to live in काशी till death, are expected to observe the rules of धर्म very strictly and avoid all types of sins.
A very important aspect of पिल्ग्रिमगे to काशी is the pañcakrośī-parikrama on foot. Starting from the Maṇikarṇikā-ghāṭ, the pilgrim has to walk about 80 kms. (50 miles), in a semicircle, coming back to the same point at the end. The journey is to be covered in six days, offering one’s worship at the temples on the way and also piṇḍas (obsequial offerings to the manes) at the village Kapiladhārā.
Kāśī is famous for the various seats of learning. The Banaras Hindu University (BHU) and the काशी Vidyāpīṭha are the two most well-known institutions of this type.

Kāśyapa Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
It is a dharmasūtra work, attributed to the sage कश्यप, quoted by other writers like बौधायन (600-300 B. C.), and also later writers.
The work not available now, seems to have dealt with the usual topics of धर्मशास्त्रस् like daily duties, śrāddha (obsequial rites), अशौच (ceremonial impurity), प्रायश्चित्त (expiation for sins) and so on.
A manuscript discovered a few years back, called Kaśyapasmṛti is in prose and deals with the duties of the householders, expiation for polluting public places like wells, ponds and temples, expiations for killing cows and other animals as also other sins, rules concerning mourning after death, purification of vessels of wood and metal and so on.

kaṣāya
(‘that which upsets’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘kaṣāya’ is used in several senses depending upon the particular branch of knowledge.
If it means astringent taste in the culinary sciences, it represents the boiled and decanted essence of medicinal herbs, in आयुर्वेद.
In the philosophical works, however, the word is used to indicate those weaknesses and impurities of मिन्द् which are obstacles to spiritual evolution. They may be either in a potential state or manifested fully. For instance: राग (attachment) and द्वेष (hatred). It is only the person who has transcended the kaṣāyas that is fit for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.

Kaśyapa
------------------------------------------
The sage कश्यप has been mentioned not only in the Ṛgveda (9.114.2) but also in the Rāmāyaṇa (Bālakāṇḍa 70 and 75), the Mahābhārata (Ādiparva 63), the Viṣṇupurāṇa (1.15 and 21) and the Bhāgavata (4.1). Whether all these Kaśyapas are one and the same or are different, it is difficult to say.
He was the son of the sage मरीचि and grandson of ब्रह्मा, the creator. His मोथेर् was कला, a daughter of कर्दम and देवहूति. He had married the 13 daughters of दक्ष and thereby became the ड़थेर् of the देवस् (gods), असुरस् (demons), सिद्धस्, गन्धर्वस्, yakṣas (all these being demigods), नागस् (reptiles) and other animals; i.e., the whole च्रेअतिओन्. That is why, when the गोत्र (lineage) of a person is not known, he is permitted to say ‘Kāśyapagotra’. (This is necessary in the performance of religious ceremonies.)
Kaśyapa and अदिति (the eldest wife) were reborn as दशरथ and कौसल्या, Vasudeva and देवकी since they had prayed to the Lord विष्णु that he be born as their son.
